title: Protective Perturbations Must Survive the Resize: Scale-Robust Image Immunization against Malicious Editing

paper.title: Protective Perturbations Must Survive the Resize: Scale-Robust Image Immunization against Malicious Editing
paper.abstract:
Abstract Protective perturbations aim to stop malicious instruction-guided editing of personal photos, but they are optimized and evaluated at the editor’s working resolution, whereas shared photos have 10 megapixels or more and editors first downscale them by an unknown factor.
We model this resize as a frequency-selective channel.
In this model, a perturbation computed at the native resolution decays with the downscaling factor and is weak even without a resize, and a perturbation computed at a fixed working resolution protects only a window of scales.
The best worst-case protection over an unknown range of scales degrades only logarithmically with the width of the range, and averaging over scales does not reach it.
Guided by this analysis, we propose SRIM, which samples a grid of anchor scales covering the whole range, with weights that favor the currently weakest scale, at the cost of standard expectation over transformation.
On full-resolution photos of 9 to 30 megapixels and downscaling factors from 2 to 8, SRIM raises the worst-case disruption of FLUX.2-klein edits from 0.192 LPIPS, attained by the strongest published protection, to 0.463.
At equal visibility, it roughly doubles the protection.
The same protected photos also protect against the 9B model and against FLUX.2-dev, with worst cases of 0.450 and 0.386 against at most 0.184 for published protections, and SRIM leads on InstructPix2Pix as well.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Instruction-guided editors built on diffusion and flow-matching transformers, such as FLUX.1 Kontext [ 6 ] , Qwen-Image-Edit [ 19 ] , and FLUX.2, turn a single photograph into a convincing forgery with one sentence of text. Since these editors are open and cheap to run, anyone who can download a personal photo can also falsify it. A growing line of work therefore asks the owner of a photo to immunize it before sharing: a small adversarial perturbation is added so that any later edit of the image fails [ 13 , 7 , 8 , 21 , 3 , 18 , 5 , 15 ] . We study this task in the setting in which it is used. The owner shares the photo at its native resolution, typically 10 to 30 megapixels, while the editor resizes its input to between 0.25 0.25 and 4 4 megapixels before encoding it. The editor therefore sees the protected photo only after an antialiased downscaling by a factor s s that the owner does not know. In general, existing protections can be roughly divided into two categories. Protections of the first category are computed at one resolution: either the editor’s working resolution, typically 512 × 512 512\times 512 pixels for Stable Diffusion editors and about one megapixel for diffusion transformers, or the native resolution of the photo. Protections of the second category average the perturbation over random transformations with expectation over transformation (EOT) [ 1 , 23 ] . Despite their effectiveness at the editor’s working resolution, both categories lose most of their effect at the scales that real editors use. A single 0.5 × 0.5\times resize already removes most of the protection of existing methods [ 16 ] . As shown in , once the photo is downscaled, the strongest published protection with EOT no longer stops the edit. We argue that this limitation stems from a latent assumption of existing protections: that the editor sees the protected image at the scale for which the protection was optimized, or, with EOT, that protecting the average scale protects every scale. However, this assumption does not hold when an editor downscales the photo by a factor that the owner does not know. Viewed as a frequency-selective channel, the resize discards most of a native-resolution perturbation and keeps a fixed-resolution perturbation effective only in a narrow window of scales. When the protection is averaged over scales, the scales at the ends of the range remain uncovered ( Sec. 4 ). This raises an intriguing question: is it possible to protect a photo at every scale at which an unknown editor may view it, at the cost of existing protections? The answer to this question is positive. Instead of optimizing the protection for one expected scale or for the average over scales, we optimize it for the scale at which it is currently weakest. In general, our method, dubbed SRIM (Scale-Robust IMmunization), consists of two components. First, it places anchor scales on a grid that covers the whole range implied by the photo size, which addresses the first limitation ( i.e . , the narrow window of fixed-resolution protection). Second, at each step it draws one anchor from a distribution that tracks the currently weakest scale, in the spirit of group distributionally robust optimization [ 12 ] , which addresses the second limitation ( i.e . , the uncovered ends of the range under averaging). Since each step encodes a single downscaled copy, SRIM costs the same as EOT and needs no knowledge of the editor’s preprocessing. We also provide theoretical analysis showing that, under a linearized spectral model, the best worst-case protection degrades only logarithmically with the width of the scale range, whereas averaging over scales does not attain it ( Sec. 5.1 ). In conclusion, the main contributions of this paper are four-fold. • We revisit image immunization under the resize that editors apply to shared photos, and reveal the root cause of its failure: the protection is optimized for a scale, or an average of scales, that the editor does not use. • Based on our analysis, we propose SRIM, which covers the whole range of scales with anchors and spends each step on the currently weakest one, at the cost of EOT. • We theoretically analyze protection under an unknown resize. We show that native-resolution protection decays with the downscaling factor and that fixed-resolution protection covers only a window of scales. We also show that the best worst-case protection degrades only logarithmically with the scale range, and that averaging over scales does not attain it. • We conduct experiments on full-resolution photos and four editors, including FLUX.2-dev. On the FLUX.2 editors, SRIM raises the worst-case disruption of edits to 2.3 to 2.4 times that of the strongest published protection. On FLUX.2-klein, it also remains the strongest under resampling filters and input purification that it does not model.

sections.heading: Image immunization against malicious editing
sections.text: PhotoGuard [ 13 ] introduced protective perturbations against latent diffusion editing, either by pushing the encoder latent toward a target or by attacking the full diffusion process. AdvDM [ 7 ] and Mist [ 8 ] maximize the denoising loss and add a textural latent loss, and score distillation makes these attacks cheaper [ 21 ] . Guo et al . [ 5 ] showed that attacking only the posterior of the variational autoencoder (VAE) already disrupts latent diffusion editing and transfers across models that share the autoencoder. DiffusionGuard [ 3 ] targets inpainting with mask augmentation, FaceLock [ 18 ] optimizes against face recognition features, and DeContext [ 15 ] weakens the attention pathways that carry context in diffusion transformer editors. Related protections target personalization [ 17 , 14 , 22 ] and cross-model transfer [ 25 ] ; a recent survey covers the area [ 24 ] . All of these methods compute the perturbation at the resolution at which the editor will see the image. Our analysis concerns the step they leave out: the resize between the shared photo and the editor’s input.

sections.heading: Robustness of protections
sections.text: Protections are known to be fragile under compression, purification, and resizing [ 9 , 16 , 27 ] . The standard remedy is expectation over transformation (EOT) [ 1 ] , and EOLT learns the transformation distribution instead of sampling it uniformly [ 23 ] . AntiPure adds frequency guidance to resist diffusion purification [ 22 ] . We show that for an unknown resize the relevant quantity is the worst case over scales rather than the average, derive its optimal value, and give a method that targets it at the cost of EOT.

sections.heading: Resampling and adversarial perturbations
sections.text: Image-scaling attacks exploit downsampling in the opposite direction: they hide a target image that appears only after the victim resizes the input [ 20 , 10 ] . Low-frequency adversarial perturbations are known to transfer better and to survive defenses that remove high frequencies [ 4 ] . Our transfer-function analysis explains why low-frequency content matters for protection against editors in particular: the editor discards the top of its own frequency band, so energy placed there is wasted even before any resize.

sections.text: The standard remedy, EOT [ 1 ] , draws the scale at random and maximizes the average protection. It relies on the latent assumption that protecting the average scale protects every scale. Theorem 4 (EOT is not minimax) . The maximizer of the average of ρ s \rho_{s} over log-uniform s s concentrates its energy at a single native frequency ω † \omega^{\dagger} . With our objective, EOT is flat in the middle of the range on FLUX.2-klein (0.473 to 0.518 for s ≤ 6 s\leq 6 ) but drops to 0.382 at s = 8 s=8 , the largest downscaling. The above analyses reveal that the root cause is the same in all three cases: each protection is optimized for a scale, or for an average of scales, that does not represent the scale the editor uses. This motivates us to optimize the protection for the scale at which it is currently weakest, rather than for one expected scale or for the average.

sections.heading: 5 SRIM: Worst-Case Scale-Robust Protection
sections.text: Motivated by Sec. 4 , SRIM optimizes the worst scale rather than the average. A direct minimax would evaluate every scale at every step and multiply the cost by the number of scales and the pixel count of the larger ones. Instead, SRIM keeps the cost of EOT by drawing one scale per step. It draws this scale from a distribution that concentrates on the scales where the protection is currently weakest, in the spirit of group distributionally robust optimization [ 12 ] .

sections.heading: Objective and settings
sections.text: We maximize the relative latent deviation ( 1 ) of the editor family’s VAE encoder, an untargeted objective that needs neither a target image nor the denoiser. Because each step encodes one downscaled copy, a step costs less than one encoder pass at the native resolution. The memory stays below that of encoding a 5.1-megapixel image (the largest anchor with its jitter). In contrast, computing a perturbation at the native resolution of a 12-megapixel photo exceeds the memory of a 48 GB GPU ( Sec. 6 ).

sections.heading: Editors
sections.text: We attack four instruction-guided editors: FLUX.2-klein in its 4B and 9B versions (4 sampling steps), FLUX.2-dev (28 steps), and InstructPix2Pix [ 2 ] (50 steps). The three FLUX.2 editors share one VAE, which serves as the surrogate for all of them, so the same protected photos are evaluated on each; InstructPix2Pix uses its own VAE. The protected photo is downscaled with the Lanczos filter by s ∈ { 2 , 3 , 4 , 6 , 8 } s\in\{2,3,4,6,8\} (working widths 2048 to 512 pixels) and edited with two fixed instructions and seeds. This grid is the same for every photo, whereas the range covered by the protections depends on the photo size ( Sec. 3 ), so for some photos the smallest or the largest factor lies outside the covered range. InstructPix2Pix, trained at 512 pixels, works at s ∈ { 4 , 6 , 8 } s\in\{4,6,8\} , and FLUX.2-dev at s ∈ { 3 , 4 , 6 , 8 } s\in\{3,4,6,8\} , since at s = 2 s=2 its input exceeds its working range for portrait photos. On FLUX.2-dev, a 32-billion-parameter model, we compare with the EOT variants and PCA@1MP. Implementation details are in Section S2 of the supplementary material, and Section S3 reports per-scale results for every editor, the budget sweep behind Figure 5 , the visibility of each protection, and edits of more photos at more scales. sections.heading: Metrics
sections.text: Protection is measured by how far the edit of the protected photo departs from the edit of the clean photo: LPIPS [ 26 ] (higher is better), PSNR and SSIM (lower is better), and CLIP image similarity [ 11 ] (lower is better). We report the average over scales and the worst case over scales, the quantity the owner cares about.

sections.heading: Baselines
sections.text: We compare with protections that, like ours, need only a public surrogate model and no training: PhotoGuard [ 13 ] (encoder attack), Mist [ 8 ] (textural loss), and PCA [ 5 ] , each run on the same VAE as our method. We do not include protections that attack the denoiser of one editor [ 7 , 21 , 15 ] . On the FLUX.2 editors, they would backpropagate through a transformer of 4 to 32 billion parameters at every step, and they are tied to that editor, whereas a VAE attack serves every editor that shares the autoencoder. A user holding a high-resolution photo can apply them in two ways: at about one megapixel with the perturbation upsampled back ( @1MP ), or at the native resolution, which exceeds the memory of a 48 GB L40S GPU for 12-megapixel photos. We also equip each baseline with EOT over the same scale range ( +EOT ), the standard remedy for transformations, and include EOT with our objective as the strongest such variant. All methods share ϵ = 4 / 255 \epsilon=4/255 , 200 steps, and the step-size schedule.

sections.heading: 6.1 Main results
sections.text: Table 1 reports the main comparison. Applied at about one megapixel, as a user would apply them to a downscaled copy, the published protections lose most of their effect once the editor’s working resolution departs from one megapixel. On the FLUX.2 editors, their worst case over scales is at most 0.097, consistent with the scale window of Theorem 3 . EOT recovers part of the loss, but the best published method with EOT, Mist+EOT, still reaches only 0.192 on FLUX.2-klein 4B, 0.184 on the 9B model, and 0.166 on FLUX.2-dev in the worst case. SRIM raises the worst case to 0.463, 0.450, and 0.386 on these three editors, which is 2.3 to 2.4 times the best published protection. It raises the worst case to 0.269 on InstructPix2Pix and gives the highest average on every editor. Because the three FLUX.2 editors share one VAE, the same protected photos transfer from the 4B model, the smallest, to the 9B model and to FLUX.2-dev, whose transformer is eight times larger. The protection weakens with the size of the denoiser but keeps its margin over the baselines. Figure 3 shows selected real edits at the largest downscaling: the edits of photos protected by published methods stay close to the edit of the unprotected photo, while SRIM disrupts them. The ablation without worst-case sampling (Ours-obj.+EOT) is close to SRIM on average but loses at the extreme scales, as Theorem 4 predicts for averaging over scales. Its worst case is 0.382, 0.367, and 0.319 on the FLUX.2 editors and 0.250 on InstructPix2Pix. Figure 4 breaks the comparison down by scale and shows the three behaviors of Sec. 4 on every editor. The protection computed at one megapixel decays monotonically as s s grows, as predicted by Theorem 3 . EOT with our objective matches or slightly exceeds SRIM in the middle of the range but drops at s = 8 s=8 , as predicted by Theorem 4 . SRIM stays the flattest across scales, and its margin is largest at the largest downscaling.

sections.heading: Protection at equal visibility
sections.text: At a fixed ϵ \epsilon , SRIM uses more of the budget than the baselines. It is therefore more visible when the photo is viewed at one megapixel (LPIPS 0.207 against 0.067 to 0.153 at ϵ = 4 / 255 \epsilon=4/255 ). Figure 5 therefore compares the methods at equal visibility. At a visibility of 0.10, SRIM reaches a worst-case edit LPIPS of 0.341, against 0.159 for the best published method (PhotoGuard+EOT). At equal PSNR, the gap is similar: SRIM at ϵ = 2 / 255 \epsilon=2/255 (43.3 dB) already exceeds every published baseline at ϵ = 8 / 255 \epsilon=8/255 (at most 0.246 at about 33.5 dB). At a quarter of the budget, SRIM is less visible than the best published protection at ϵ = 8 / 255 \epsilon=8/255 (43 against 33 dB) and still disrupts the edit far more (0.60 and 0.63 against 0.14 and 0.24).

sections.heading: Cost
sections.text: On one L40S GPU, protecting a test photo (17 megapixels on average) takes 176 s with SRIM, 134 to 155 s for the EOT variants, and 59 s for the methods applied at one megapixel. Computing a baseline at the native resolution ran out of memory for most photos on the same GPU, and the one run that fit took 57 minutes.

sections.heading: 7 Conclusion
sections.text: Protective perturbations are computed for the image an editor sees, but owners share photos that current editors first downscale by a factor the owner does not know. We showed that this resize decides whether a protection works. A perturbation computed at the native resolution decays with the downscaling factor, and one computed at a fixed working resolution covers only a window of scales. Averaging over scales leaves the ends of the range exposed, while the best worst-case protection degrades only logarithmically with the width of the range. SRIM covers the scale range with anchors and spends its steps on the currently weakest one, at the cost of EOT. On four editors, it gives the strongest worst-case protection of full-resolution photos. We hope that evaluating protections under the preprocessing that editors apply becomes the default for image immunization.

sections.heading: Photos and splits
sections.text: We use the Unsplash Lite dataset and keep photos with at least 12 megapixels and an aspect ratio of at most 1.8 1.8 (19,232 eligible photos). Photos are ordered by the SHA-1 hash of their identifier, split into people and scenes by keywords in their descriptions, and resized to a width of 4096 pixels. The first 8 photos of each category form the development set, the next 20 of each category were used once each to confirm the method before testing, and the remaining 80 of each category form the test set (160 photos). Images are center-cropped to multiples of 16 pixels.

sections.heading: Editors
sections.text: FLUX.2-klein (4B and 9B) runs 4 steps with guidance 1.0; FLUX.2-dev runs 28 steps with guidance 4.0; InstructPix2Pix runs 50 steps with image guidance 1.5 and text guidance 7.5. Each editor receives the protected photo after Lanczos downscaling (Python Imaging Library) to the working size given by s s , rounded to multiples of 16 pixels, and edits with fixed seeds. Instructions: “Turn this photo into a watercolor painting” and “Make it snowy winter”. FLUX.2-klein 4B and 9B use s ∈ { 2 , 3 , 4 , 6 , 8 } s\in\{2,3,4,6,8\} and both instructions on all 160 test photos. InstructPix2Pix uses s ∈ { 4 , 6 , 8 } s\in\{4,6,8\} and both instructions on all 160 photos. FLUX.2-dev uses s ∈ { 3 , 4 , 6 , 8 } s\in\{3,4,6,8\} and both instructions on all 160 photos, with PhotoGuard+EOT, Mist+EOT, PCA+EOT, PCA@1MP, Ours-obj.+EOT, and SRIM. The 9B model runs with CPU offloading of the text encoder and transformer; for FLUX.2-dev, the instruction embeddings are computed once and the transformer is split across two GPUs, which leaves the computation unchanged.

sections.heading: Metrics
sections.text: LPIPS uses the AlexNet backbone [ 26 ] ; CLIP image and text similarities use ViT-L/14 [ 11 ] . All metrics compare the edit of the protected photo with the edit of the clean photo under the same instruction and seed.

sections.heading: Baselines
sections.text: PhotoGuard (encoder attack), Mist (textural loss), and PCA are re-implemented on the editor’s VAE following the official code. PhotoGuard minimizes the latent distance to the latent of a gray image, and Mist minimizes the distance to the latent of the Mist target pattern resized to the input size. PCA ascends the posterior-collapse objective with v = 10 − 8 v=10^{-8} . All baselines use the same budget ( ϵ = 4 / 255 \epsilon=4/255 ), 200 sign-gradient steps with step size ϵ / 4 \epsilon/4 and cosine decay, and the same EOT scale range as SRIM in their +EOT variants. The @1MP variants run at a working size of about one megapixel and upsample the perturbation bicubically, clipped to the budget. Native-resolution application on the test photos exceeds 44 GB of GPU memory for most photos.

Report Issue Back to Abstract Download PDF Contents Reading mode Colour theme License: arXiv.org perpetual non-exclusive license arXiv:2610.07464v1 [cs.CV] 05 Oct 2026 Protective Perturbations Must Survive the Resize: Scale-Robust Image Immunization against Malicious Editing Zhongliang Guo Yan Lin Yifei Qian Daizong Liu Affiliation: University of Aberdeen Newcastle University University of Nottingham Wuhan University Abstract Protective perturbations aim to stop malicious instruction-guided editing of personal photos, but they are optimized and evaluated at the editor’s working resolution, whereas shared photos have 10 megapixels or more and editors first downscale them by an unknown factor. We model this resize as a frequency-selective channel. In this model, a perturbation computed at the native resolution decays with the downscaling factor and is weak even without a resize, and a perturbation computed at a fixed working resolution protects only a window of scales. The best worst-case protection over an unknown range of scales degrades only logarithmically with the width of the range, and averaging over scales does not reach it. Guided by this analysis, we propose SRIM, which samples a grid of anchor scales covering the whole range, with weights that favor the currently weakest scale, at the cost of standard expectation over transformation. On full-resolution photos of 9 to 30 megapixels and downscaling factors from 2 to 8, SRIM raises the worst-case disruption of FLUX.2-klein edits from 0.192 LPIPS, attained by the strongest published protection, to 0.463. At equal visibility, it roughly doubles the protection. The same protected photos also protect against the 9B model and against FLUX.2-dev, with worst cases of 0.450 and 0.386 against at most 0.184 for published protections, and SRIM leads on InstructPix2Pix as well. 1 Introduction Instruction-guided editors built on diffusion and flow-matching transformers, such as FLUX.1 Kontext [ 6 ] , Qwen-Image-Edit [ 19 ] , and FLUX.2, turn a single photograph into a convincing forgery with one sentence of text. Since these editors are open and cheap to run, anyone who can download a personal photo can also falsify it. A growing line of work therefore asks the owner of a photo to immunize it before sharing: a small adversarial perturbation is added so that any later edit of the image fails [ 13 , 7 , 8 , 21 , 3 , 18 , 5 , 15 ] . We study this task in the setting in which it is used. The owner shares the photo at its native resolution, typically 10 to 30 megapixels, while the editor resizes its input to between 0.25 0.25 and 4 4 megapixels before encoding it. The editor therefore sees the protected photo only after an antialiased downscaling by a factor s s that the owner does not know. In general, existing protections can be roughly divided into two categories. Protections of the first category are computed at one resolution: either the editor’s working resolution, typically 512 × 512 512	imes 512 pixels for Stable Diffusion editors and about one megapixel for diffusion transformers, or the native resolution of the photo. Protections of the second category average the perturbation over random transformations with expectation over transformation (EOT) [ 1 , 23 ] . Despite their effectiveness at the editor’s working resolution, both categories lose most of their effect at the scales that real editors use. A single 0.5 × 0.5	imes resize already removes most of the protection of existing methods [ 16 ] . As shown in , once the photo is downscaled, the strongest published protection with EOT no longer stops the edit. We argue that this limitation stems from a latent assumption of existing protections: that the editor sees the protected image at the scale for which the protection was optimized, or, with EOT, that protecting the average scale protects every scale. However, this assumption does not hold when an editor downscales the photo by a factor that the owner does not know. Viewed as a frequency-selective channel, the resize discards most of a native-resolution perturbation and keeps a fixed-resolution perturbation effective only in a narrow window of scales. When the protection is averaged over scales, the scales at the ends of the range remain uncovered ( Sec. 4 ). This raises an intriguing question: is it possible to protect a photo at every scale at which an unknown editor may view it, at the cost of existing protections? The answer to this question is positive. Instead of optimizing the protection for one expected scale or for the average over scales, we optimize it for the scale at which it is currently weakest. In general, our method, dubbed SRIM (Scale-Robust IMmunization), consists of two components. First, it places anchor scales on a grid that covers the whole range implied by the photo size, which addresses the first limitation ( i.e . , the narrow window of fixed-resolution protection). Second, at each step it draws one anchor from a distribution that tracks the currently weakest scale, in the spirit of group distributionally robust optimization [ 12 ] , which addresses the second limitation ( i.e . , the uncovered ends of the range under averaging). Since each step encodes a single downscaled copy, SRIM costs the same as EOT and needs no knowledge of the editor’s preprocessing. We also provide theoretical analysis showing that, under a linearized spectral model, the best worst-case protection degrades only logarithmically with the width of the scale range, whereas averaging over scales does not attain it ( Sec. 5.1 ). In conclusion, the main contributions of this paper are four-fold. • We revisit image immunization under the resize that editors apply to shared photos, and reveal the root cause of its failure: the protection is optimized for a scale, or an average of scales, that the editor does not use. • Based on our analysis, we propose SRIM, which covers the whole range of scales with anchors and spends each step on the currently weakest one, at the cost of EOT. • We theoretically analyze protection under an unknown resize. We show that native-resolution protection decays with the downscaling factor and that fixed-resolution protection covers only a window of scales. We also show that the best worst-case protection degrades only logarithmically with the scale range, and that averaging over scales does not attain it. • We conduct experiments on full-resolution photos and four editors, including FLUX.2-dev. On the FLUX.2 editors, SRIM raises the worst-case disruption of edits to 2.3 to 2.4 times that of the strongest published protection. On FLUX.2-klein, it also remains the strongest under resampling filters and input purification that it does not model. 2 Related Work Image immunization against malicious editing PhotoGuard [ 13 ] introduced protective perturbations against latent diffusion editing, either by pushing the encoder latent toward a target or by attacking the full diffusion process. AdvDM [ 7 ] and Mist [ 8 ] maximize the denoising loss and add a textural latent loss, and score distillation makes these attacks cheaper [ 21 ] . Guo et al . [ 5 ] showed that attacking only the posterior of the variational autoencoder (VAE) already disrupts latent diffusion editing and transfers across models that share the autoencoder. DiffusionGuard [ 3 ] targets inpainting with mask augmentation, FaceLock [ 18 ] optimizes against face recognition features, and DeContext [ 15 ] weakens the attention pathways that carry context in diffusion transformer editors. Related protections target personalization [ 17 , 14 , 22 ] and cross-model transfer [ 25 ] ; a recent survey covers the area [ 24 ] . All of these methods compute the perturbation at the resolution at which the editor will see the image. Our analysis concerns the step they leave out: the resize between the shared photo and the editor’s input. Robustness of protections Protections are known to be fragile under compression, purification, and resizing [ 9 , 16 , 27 ] . The standard remedy is expectation over transformation (EOT) [ 1 ] , and EOLT learns the transformation distribution instead of sampling it uniformly [ 23 ] . AntiPure adds frequency guidance to resist diffusion purification [ 22 ] . We show that for an unknown resize the relevant quantity is the worst case over scales rather than the average, derive its optimal value, and give a method that targets it at the cost of EOT. Resampling and adversarial perturbations Image-scaling attacks exploit downsampling in the opposite direction: they hide a target image that appears only after the victim resizes the input [ 20 , 10 ] . Low-frequency adversarial perturbations are known to transfer better and to survive defenses that remove high frequencies [ 4 ] . Our transfer-function analysis explains why low-frequency content matters for protection against editors in particular: the editor discards the top of its own frequency band, so energy placed there is wasted even before any resize. 3 Problem Setup Threat model An owner shares a photo 𝒙 ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] 3 × H × W  m{x}\in[0,1]^{3	imes H	imes W} at its native resolution, typically 10 to 30 megapixels. Computing a baseline at the native resolution ran out of memory for most photos on the same GPU, and the one run that fit took 57 minutes. 7 Conclusion Protective perturbations are computed for the image an editor sees, but owners share photos that current editors first downscale by a factor the owner does not know. We showed that this resize decides whether a protection works. A perturbation computed at the native resolution decays with the downscaling factor, and one computed at a fixed working resolution covers only a window of scales. Averaging over scales leaves the ends of the range exposed, while the best worst-case protection degrades only logarithmically with the width of the range. SRIM covers the scale range with anchors and spends its steps on the currently weakest one, at the cost of EOT. On four editors, it gives the strongest worst-case protection of full-resolution photos. We hope that evaluating protections under the preprocessing that editors apply becomes the default for image immunization. References [1] A. Athalye, L. Engstrom, A. Ilyas, and K.
